title: Network Engineer: addressing, segmentation and layered fault-finding
intro: Networks fail in predictable layers. Learn to address and segment cleanly, read a config for mistakes, recognise normal and odd traffic, and walk the layers in order. Everything here runs on text you paste or on public hosts.
outcome: A clean addressing plan with no overlaps, a reviewed config, one capture explained, and a layered troubleshooting runbook.

steps.title: Plan the addressing
steps.what: Good addressing is boring: no overlaps, room to grow, one block per purpose.
how: Open Subnet and VLSM and subnet 192.168.10.0/26: read the usable hosts and the broadcast address.
Plan an office in 10.20.0.0/22 with the VLSM planner: 60 staff, 20 guests, 10 servers, two point-to-point links.
Paste your planned networks into the overlap check, then summarise the routes.
steps.done_when: A plan whose subnets don't overlap and each has spare room.
mistakes: Sizing a subnet to exactly today's hosts.
Forgetting the network and broadcast addresses.
steps.ask: How many hosts fit in a /27 and why is it 30, not 32?

steps.title: Review a device config
steps.what: Most breaches of network gear are default passwords, telnet and open management.
how: Open Config review and load the sample.
Read each high finding and say what an attacker would do with it.
Write the fix for each, then paste your fixed version and run it again.
steps.done_when: No high findings, and you can explain each fix.
mistakes: Treating 'no findings' as 'secure'.
Fixing the symptom and not the habit that caused it.
steps.ask: Why is SNMP community 'public' a problem?

steps.title: Read what is on the wire
steps.what: Traffic has shapes: handshakes, resets, scans, ARP chatter.
how: Open Packet capture and load the sample.
Find the completed TCP handshake, then the burst of SYNs to many ports.
Decide: scan, monitoring or a broken client, and what you'd check next.
steps.done_when: You can explain the finding and one alternative explanation.
mistakes: Calling one pattern an attack without context.
Capturing on a network you don't own.
steps.ask: What does a SYN without a SYN-ACK tell me?

steps.title: Test the path
steps.what: Names, then addresses, then ports: one layer at a time.
how: Open DNS and reachability and look up a site you use.
Test TCP 443 on it, then a closed port, and compare the results.
Say which layer each result rules in or out.
steps.done_when: You can say what 'open', 'closed' and 'filtered' mean.
mistakes: Testing hosts you don't own at scale.
Blaming the network for a DNS problem.
steps.ask: If ping to an IP works but the name fails, what is wrong?

steps.title: Size the pipe
steps.what: Bandwidth isn't throughput: window, latency and overhead decide the speed.
how: Open Calculators and find how long 200 GB takes over 100 Mbps at 85% efficiency.
Enter 1000 Mbps and 80 ms with a 64 KB window and read the limit.
Decide what you'd change to fill the link.
steps.done_when: You can explain why a fast link can still be slow.
mistakes: Using megabits and megabytes interchangeably.
steps.ask: Why can one TCP stream fail to fill a long fast link?

steps.title: Keep a method and a reference
steps.what: The method is the skill; the table is just memory.
how: Open Reference and read the troubleshooting method.
Write your own one-page runbook for 'the internet is down', layer by layer.
Look up five ports and what each should never be exposed for.
steps.done_when: A runbook someone else could follow.
mistakes: Skipping the physical layer.
Changing three things at once.
steps.ask: Walk me through troubleshooting 'I can't reach the file server'.

steps.title: Build and check VLANs, trunks and routes
steps.what: Most switching tickets are one of four faults: wrong mode, mismatched native VLAN, a VLAN not allowed on the trunk, or a VLAN missing from one switch. Learn to write the config and to read two configs side by side.
how: Open Config generators > VLAN and router-on-a-stick, keep the two default VLANs and press Generate. Read each switch and router line and say what it does.
Add a loopback such as 1.1.1.1. Explain why a second router still cannot ping it until it has a route.
Switch to Trunk checker, run the sample and fix the two faults by editing switch B until it reports none.
In Route selection, find the winner for 10.1.2.3 and explain why a /16 from RIP beats a /8 from a static route.
Use the Cable chooser for a 10 Gbps run of 80 m and say why Cat 6a, not Cat 7, is the usual answer.
Read the Devices, DHCP and protocols tab and write down the slips in the posters.
steps.done_when: You can generate a router-on-a-stick config and explain every line, and find a native VLAN mismatch by reading two configs.
mistakes: Using VLAN 1 as the native VLAN on both ends because it works.
Listing a VLAN on the router but leaving it off the trunk's allowed list.
Pasting a generated config into a production device without reading it.
steps.ask: Why would a router-on-a-stick link become a bottleneck, and what replaces it?

steps.title: Set up a DHCP and DNS server (dnsmasq)
steps.what: A small network needs something to hand out addresses and answer names. dnsmasq does both with a few lines of configuration.
how: Open Network > Generators > DHCP server (dnsmasq) and build a config for 192.168.50.0/24 with a range, a gateway, one reservation and one DNS name.
Read each line and say what it does and what a client would get from it.
Paste it into the checker and confirm it is clean.
Load the sample bad config into the checker and fix the three errors on paper.
In a virtual machine, run dnsmasq --test, restart the service and watch the journal while a test client asks for an address.
steps.done_when: You can explain Discover, Offer, Request and Acknowledge, and tell which line gives clients their gateway.
mistakes: Running a second DHCP server on the same network.
Putting the gateway inside the dynamic range.
Forgetting that systemd-resolved already uses port 53 on many Linux systems.
steps.ask: A client gets an address but cannot reach the internet. What do you check in the DHCP settings?

steps.title: Design a small network on paper before buying anything
steps.what: Good design starts with requirements, not devices. You gather what the business needs, assess what exists, set measurable goals, design the logical network (addresses, VLANs, zones), then choose devices, plan security and resilience, and write it all down.
how: Open Network > Network design > Design steps and read the nine steps. Notice which ones the source skipped.
Open Design planner, keep the sample groups, and press Plan it.
Read the address plan. Why is each subnet bigger than its host count? Change growth to 0 and compare.
Turn guest Wi-Fi and remote access on and off. Which zones and risks appear?
Switch redundancy to none and full and watch the device counts and risks change.
Write a one-page design for a real place: requirements, address plan, device list, risks and a rollback plan.
steps.done_when: You can walk through the design steps in order, size a subnet with growth, and explain why a diagram and an address plan are produced before any purchase.
mistakes: Buying hardware before the requirements and the address plan exist.
Sizing subnets for today's hosts with no growth.
Forgetting a rollback plan and a pilot.
Leaving guest Wi-Fi on a route to internal subnets.
steps.ask: I have 60 staff in two floors and a warehouse. Walk me through the address plan and how many access points and switches I should price.

steps.title: Learn the networking vocabulary, protocols and default ports
steps.what: Hubs, switches, routers, TCP, UDP, DNS, DHCP and the rest are the shared language of every network job. The ports table is worth knowing cold, along with the fact that ports are defaults, not rules.
how: Open Network design > Glossary and search 'wireless'. Check WMAN and WPAN carefully.
Open Ports and read the table. Say out loud which are clear text and which are encrypted.
For each of hub, switch and router, say what it looks at (nothing, MAC address, IP address).
Pick one protocol (DNS) and say which transport it uses and why.
Use the questions at the end of this step as a spaced-review set.
steps.done_when: You can state the job, the transport and the default port of the common protocols and correct the mistakes in the source glossary.
mistakes: Learning ports as law. A service can listen on any port.
Mixing up SFTP (SSH, port 22) and FTPS.
Treating Telnet and FTP as acceptable because they still work.
Calling SMB 137 to 139; modern SMB is TCP 445.
steps.ask: Quiz me on twelve protocols: name, port, TCP or UDP, and whether it is encrypted.
